summary: Extends IMAP so that UTF-8 characters can be used in user names, mail addresses and message headers, supporting international email. It replaced RFC 5738 and was in turn replaced by RFC 9755.

eli5.summary: Lets email programs handle names and words written with any letters, not just the plain English ones.

questions: how to use international characters in imap
how does imap handle international characters
how to enable utf-8 in imap
subtitle: International characters in email servers and addresses

tldr.problem: Email systems originally worked only with ASCII characters, making it impossible to use international characters in usernames, email addresses, and message headers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6855 extends IMAP to accept UTF-8 encoding for these fields, letting servers advertise UTF-8 support via the UTF8=ACCEPT and UTF8=ONLY capabilities.
tldr.outcome: Email can now use any Unicode character, but servers must handle legacy clients that only understand ASCII. RFC 9755 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 9755 updated this specification in October 2024. The core mechanism remains the same: IMAP servers advertise UTF-8 support and clients enable it before using international characters.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6855 extends the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) to support UTF-8 encoded international characters. This is part of the Email Address Internationalization (EAI) effort described in RFC 6530, which also updates IMAP for UTF-8 in message headers (RFC 6532).

The RFC defines two new IMAP capabilities. UTF8=ACCEPT means the server can open mailboxes containing internationalized messages and return UTF-8 in responses. UTF8=ONLY means the server requires UTF-8 support from clients. This RFC replaces the earlier experimental RFC 5738.
sections.eli5: This is a recipe for email servers to say 'I speak many languages' and for email clients to understand them.

sections.title: UTF-8 in IMAP Quoted-Strings
sections.content:
The base IMAP specification forbids 8-bit characters in atoms or quoted-strings; UTF-8 strings had to be sent as literals. RFC 6855 allows UTF-8 quoted-strings when the server advertises UTF8=ACCEPT, making it simpler to send UTF-8 data.

A client must use the ENABLE command with UTF8=ACCEPT to tell the server it accepts UTF-8 in responses. The server MUST reject any octet sequences with the high bit set that do not comply with UTF-8 syntax. The server MUST NOT send UTF-8 in quoted-strings unless the client has enabled this capability.

Mailbox names can use UTF-8 characters, but must comply with the Net-Unicode Definition and cannot contain control characters, the delete character, or line/paragraph separators.
sections.eli5: Servers and clients shake hands to agree on using international letters in text. If they agree, they can skip a slow dance step that was needed before.

sections.title: The APPEND Command and UTF-8 Messages
sections.content:
RFC 6855 defines a UTF8 data extension for the APPEND command, used to upload messages to the server. A client sending a message with UTF-8 headers MUST use the UTF8() syntax: UTF8 (literal8). If the server supports CATENATE, the same extension works for catenating messages.

If the server supports UTF8=ACCEPT but the client has not issued ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT, the server MUST reject with a NO response any APPEND command that contains 8-bit characters in message header fields. Clients that need UTF-8 usernames or passwords cannot use the plain LOGIN command; they must use AUTHENTICATE, which already handles UTF-8.
sections.eli5: When uploading a message with international letters, the client says 'this is UTF-8 data' so the server knows what to expect.

sections.title: Dealing with Legacy Clients
sections.content:
The main challenge is that not all clients support UTF-8. When a message requiring SMTPUTF8 (an international email sender) arrives and a legacy client tries to read it, the server has difficult choices: hide the message, send error notifications, or create a downgraded surrogate of the original.

These surrogates are problematic: they usually cannot be replied to without losing information, and digital signatures computed over the original fail verification. The safest approach is for systems receiving international email to ensure all components (IMAP clients, POP clients, webmail) are upgraded appropriately.

RFC 6857 and RFC 6858 define standardized downgrading algorithms if surrogates are necessary. Implementors should use one of these to minimize damage.
sections.eli5: Old email programs don't understand fancy letters. Servers can pretend the message says something simpler, but the result is never perfect.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
The security considerations of UTF-8 (RFC 3629) and SASLprep (RFC 4013) apply, particularly for usernames and passwords. Beyond that, RFC 6855 does not significantly change IMAP's security posture.

Special care is needed when the same user accesses a server via different methods (IMAP, POP, webmail) or different client capabilities. If a server returns the same UIDVALIDITY to both legacy and UTF-8-aware clients, an upgraded client MUST discard its cache of previously downloaded messages to avoid inconsistency.
sections.eli5: Mixing old and new email programs accessing the same mailbox can be confusing. Clear communication helps avoid problems.
